extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (metaphysics/epistemology), esp. those studying Locke's Essay
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria and conceptual standards for understanding and assessing 'relation', 'cause and effect', and 'identity' as presented in a philosophical treatise. Useful for analyzing when a term or phenomenon counts as a relation, how causes and effects are distinguished, and what grounds identity and personal identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation as mental reference beyond the named subject
rubrics_metrics.description: A name (or idea) is relative when, by giving it, the mind is led to something beyond the thing named; the denomination implies respect to something distinct from the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: calling Caius 'husband' or 'whiter' leads the mind to another person (wife) or another property (comparative whiteness). If a term necessarily leads the mind to ideas not contained in the subject, it is a relative term. Conversely, terms that do not lead beyond the subject (e.g., 'a man', 'black') are absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlative terms signal obvious relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative words that have correlative counterparts (father/son, husband/wife, bigger/less) make relations obvious because the correlatives reciprocally evoke one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where languages provide correlative names, people readily perceive the relation; in languages lacking a correlative, the same relation might be less readily apprehended (e.g., 'concubine' without a correlative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seemingly absolute terms can conceal tacit relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some words that appear to denote absolute properties (OLD, GREAT, IMPERFECT, etc.) can in fact contain a tacit relation to some standard or comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These words may appear positive but imply a comparison (e.g., 'great' relative to a species' ordinary size). Expect apparent absolutes to sometimes function relationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations are distinct from the things related
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of relation consists in referring or comparing two distinct things; relation is extrinsic and not contained in the real existence of the related things themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If either thing is removed, the relation (and any denomination stemming from it) ceases even if the remaining thing is unchanged. Example: Caius is a father only so long as his son exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations always involve two (and only two) distinguishable items
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no relation except between two things considered as two; the whole considered as one thing is positive, while its parts may be relative to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A relation presupposes two ideas or things and a ground/occasion for their comparison (e.g., parts of a triangle compared yield relational descriptions, but the triangle as a whole is an absolute idea).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anything (all ideas) is capable of almost infinite relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Every idea—simple, compound, substance, or mode—can be considered in relation to many other ideas, producing a near-infinite number of possible relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: a single man can be father, brother, general, enemy, Englishman, etc.; relations arise whenever the mind compares that thing to others in any respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of relations can be clearer than ideas of substances
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative ideas (e.g., paternity, friendship) are often more distinct in the mind than complex ideas of substances (e.g., 'man', 'God'), because a single simple idea can ground a relation while many ideas are needed to form a substance-conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: one can have a clearer idea of 'father' than of 'man' because the notion of paternity may depend on a single action or simple idea; thus relative words can yield more perfect mental ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: All relations ultimately terminate in simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the most remote-seeming relational notions (including cause/effect) are ultimately composed from simple ideas derived from sensation or reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing any relation, trace it back to simple sensory or reflective ideas; the text illustrates this by preparing to analyze cause and effect in terms of sensation/reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms that lead the mind beyond the subject are relative (restatement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any word that necessarily leads the mind to ideas other than what is contained in the thing denoted is a relative word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: FATHER, BROTHER, KING, HUSBAND, BLACKER, MERRIER; absolute examples: MAN, BLACK, MERRY, THIRSTY (these do not imply something exterior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of cause and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Cause: that which produces any simple or complex idea; Effect: that which is produced. The idea arises from observing that qualities or substances begin to exist through the operation of something else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: heat (cause) producing fluidity in wax (effect); fire (cause) producing ashes (effect). The mind designates as cause whatever it considers to conduce to the production of a new idea or thing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of productions: creation, generation, making, alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Different origins of effects are distinguished: Creation = entirely new being (in rerum natura); Generation = new composite from pre-existing particles by natural internal principle; Making = artificial assembly via external agent/sensible separation; Alteration = production of a new simple idea in a subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to distinguish kinds of cause/effect relations (natural generation vs artificial making vs alteration of qualities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal and spatial relations as foundations for many denominations
rubrics_metrics.description: Words relating to time (WHEN, HOW LONG) and place are relational: statements of duration or temporal location express relations between durations or points and a chosen measurement standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Queen Elizabeth lived sixty-nine years' expresses a relation of her existence-duration to the standard 'year'; the date '1066' situates an event as a distance from a chosen epoch. Expect temporal/place terms to be fundamentally relational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms like 'young' and 'old' are relative to mental standards of duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives commonly thought positive (young, old) are relational because they compare an individual's age to an idea of ordinary duration for that species or kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus a 'young' man at twenty, a 'very young' child at seven; different species have different standards (a horse old at 20, a dog old at 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Size, strength, necessity expressions are often relational
rubrics_metrics.description: Words denoting bulk (great/little), strength (weak/strong), or terms like 'necessary' are relative because they compare to some standard idea the mind holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural and species standards affect application (a 'great' horse to a Welshman may be 'little' to a Fleming). 'Necessary' denotes relation to a purpose or future use (e.g., 'necessary stores').

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity defined by existence at determinate time and place
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity consists in considering something as existing at a determinate time and place and comparing it with itself at another time/place; one thing cannot be two things at the same time/place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identity requires sameness of the ideas attributed across the compared times; if the ideas differ, the things are diverse. From this follows that one thing cannot have two beginnings of existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of substances determined by their beginning in time/place
rubrics_metrics.description: For substances (God, finite intelligences, bodies), identity is fixed by a determinate time and place of beginning: God (eternal)—no doubt; finite spirits—identity by their start; bodies—identity by continuous particle-collection without addition/subtraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A particle of matter is the same so long as no matter is added or subtracted; if parts join or separate, the identity of the mass changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of modes and relations depends on their temporal nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Modes and relations (including actions like motion and thought) that exist in succession are perishing events and so cannot be identical across different times; their identity is determined by their continued existence in time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successive parts of motion or thought are distinct; continuity (or lack thereof) determines whether we speak of the same instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principium individuationis: existence (time/place) individuates
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence itself (being at a particular time and place) is the principle of individuation that fixes an entity as one individual and distinguishes it from others of the same kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine individuation, attend to the specific instant and location of existence rather than merely qualitative features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of living organisms grounded in continued organization/life, not unchanging matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A plant or animal's identity consists in a particular organization that sustains a continued life; identity can persist as new particles replace old provided the organization/life continues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an oak remains the same oak through growth and partial replacement of matter so long as the organization and life are continuous; contrast with an inert mass where identity is 'same particles'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal identity defined by consciousness continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: A person is a thinking, intelligent being capable of reason and reflection; personal identity consists solely in the continuity of consciousness (the capacity to consider oneself as the same thinking thing across times), not necessarily in sameness of substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As far as consciousness extends backwards (memory, awareness of past actions), so far personal identity reaches. Interruptions of memory do not by themselves negate personal identity; what matters is the continuity/extension of consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness inseparable from thinking and central to selfhood
rubrics_metrics.description: Consciousness always accompanies thinking and is essential to being a 'self'—one cannot perceive without perceiving that one perceives; thus consciousness is the criterion by which one is oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This grounds the claim that different substances sharing the same consciousness would constitute a single person; conversely, the same substance without continuous consciousness would not preserve personal identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal identity can persist across change of thinking-substance if consciousness continues
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the same thinking substance persists is irrelevant to personhood so long as the same consciousness (or its continuance) unites past and present thoughts; different thinking substances could, in principle, compose one person if consciousness continuity is preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: animal identity persists through changing material particles by unity of continued life; likewise personal identity may persist through changes of thinking-substance by unity of consciousness.
